cells.label: Ad filing or review
cells.text: None since January 1, 2026. The lawyer keeps a copy of each communication for 6 years, with its date, recipients and how it was sent, and hands it to the Bar’s Office of General Counsel on request (Rule 7.2(a)). For targeted letters and email, a sample, any envelope and the recipient list are kept 2 years (7.3(e)(1)).
cells.note: Rules 7.1 to 7.3 were rewritten by the Supreme Court’s order of May 13, 2025, effective January 1, 2026. Ads that ran before 2026 fell under the old 3-day filing rule.

cells.label: What each ad must include
cells.text: No general disclaimer since January 1, 2026. Each communication names a responsible lawyer and gives the city, town, county or location of a bona fide office of at least one lawyer shown, or of the firm (7.2(b)(3)-(4) and comment); says so clearly if a lawyer shown isn’t licensed in Alabama or the firm has no bona fide Alabama office (7.2(b)(1)-(2)); and every lawyer who appears is responsible for it (7.2(c)). Required statements must be easy to read or hear, and short-form ads may carry them one click away (7.2(d) and comment). Targeted letters and email are marked “ADVERTISEMENT” (7.3(f)-(i)).

cells.label: Results, testimonials and “specialist” claims
cells.text: Results only with the type of matter, objectively verifiable and not misleading (7.2(m)); no promised results (7.2(i)). Testimonials only from people with real experience of the lawyer, with paid ones disclosed (7.2(l)). No actors playing the lawyer, client portrayals only as non-speaking background, no authority-figure endorsements, and dramatizations labeled (7.2(n)-(p)). Comparisons and certification still go through Rule 7.4, which didn’t change.

cells.label: Referral services and lead generators
cells.text: Nothing of value for recommending the lawyer (7.2(h)). Allowed: the usual costs of permitted communications, a not-for-profit referral service’s usual charges, sponsorships, non-exclusive reciprocal referral agreements disclosed to the client, and nominal thank-you gifts. A lawyer doesn’t pay for another firm’s ad unless the two jointly represent the client in that matter (7.2(h)(1)). Search results aren’t manipulated or bought to divert another firm’s callers (7.2(r)).
cells.note: The rule doesn’t name lead generators; our reading is that a per-lead fee is an advertising cost only if the vendor doesn’t recommend the lawyer.

cells.label: Results, testimonials and “specialist” claims
cells.text: Banned: guarantees, quick-cash claims, undisclosed impersonations and dramatizations, spokespersons without a title, misleading statements about skill or record, and awards that came from payment or membership (§6157.2(a)). In electronic media (TV, radio and computer networks, so search and social too), results out of context, injury scenes and any money reference are presumed misleading (§6158.1), and portrayed results need their facts or a disclosure (§6158.3). “Certified specialist” only through a named, approved body (Rule 7.4). Consumers can sue for $5,000 to $100,000 per unique ad after a State Bar finding (§6157.2(c)).

cells.text: Referral services need State Bar certification (§6155), and anyone can sue an uncertified one (§6156.5) or a runner or capper (§6153) for $5,000 to $100,000 per violation. Lawyers may pay marketing vendors (Rule 7.2, comment 3). “Lawyer” includes any agent of the lawyer or firm doing business in California (§6157). San Diego County Bar Ethics Opinion 2019-2: a for-profit program that collects the consumer's flat fee and keeps a "marketing fee" is fee-sharing and an uncertified referral service.
